diagnosis.what_is_wrong: No kernel-trace evidence supports a host or workload fault explaining the reported slower coding task; the observed activity changes look like workload phase changes, not resource saturation or prolonged scheduling delay. The trace cannot establish whether the task was slower than usual, so this is a reject of an evident kernel-level incident, not proof that the symptom did not occur.
diagnosis.evidence: Across the 03:17:26.200–03:17:59.000 recording, workers used indexed full-span event counts because ctf_timeline and query_ctf returned no matches. In 03:17:26–31 versus 03:17:31–36, scheduler/futex counts fell, but scheduler runtime was only 0.193 average cores and then 0.095; during the later python3-heavy phase it was about 0.25 cores on a four-CPU host, with no measured long wake-to-run gaps in sampled raw lines. ctf_proclife showed claude and python3 present throughout; the brief 03:17:33.6–33.8 exec/exit burst was shell utilities, not service churn. ctf_procdiff comparison (03:17:26–34 versus 03:17:44–52) likewise showed changing workload composition, not an identified culprit. Disk issue/completion counts tracked with sampled latencies around 0.5–1.2 ms; sampled transmissions succeeded (rc=0), and no reclaim/OOM events were found. A finding of sustained multi-core CPU use with repeated wake-to-run delays, elevated block latency, or a clear process lifecycle failure would have falsified this conclusion; the workers checked those mechanisms and did not observe them.
diagnosis.window_evidence: No interval is supported as an incident: the early rate fall and later python3 activity correspond to changing process workload/runtime, while no corroborating resource-wait or failure signature establishes fault boundaries. The recording spans 03:17:26.200–03:17:59.000, but its activity transitions alone do not justify an incident window.
